title: Implement a trie supporting inserting a word, searching for a complete word, and checking whether any word starts with a given prefix.
shortTitle: Implement a Trie (Prefix Tree) with Insert, Search, and startsWith

s1_definition.profdef: A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree where each edge represents a character and each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that share a prefix share the same initial path. Each node holds child links and a boolean marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert, search, and prefix checks all run in time proportional to the length of the key, independent of how many words are stored.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India stores customer reference codes in a branching filing system where you follow one letter at a time. To file a code you walk letter by letter, creating a new drawer whenever one does not yet exist, and you put a little flag in the final drawer to say "a complete code ends here." To check a code you follow the same letters; if any drawer is missing the code was never filed, and even if the path exists, it only counts as a full code if the end flag is set. To check a prefix you just confirm the letter path exists, flag or no flag.
s1_definition.oneliner: Each edge is a character and each path is a prefix; a word-end flag distinguishes a full word from a mere prefix, and all operations are proportional to key length.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree where each edge represents a character and each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that share a prefix share the same initial path. Each node holds child links and a boolean marking whether a complete word ends there. Insert, search, and prefix checks all run in time proportional to the length of the key, independent of how many words are stored.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India stores customer reference codes in a branching filing system where you follow one letter at a time. To file a code you walk letter by letter, creating a new drawer whenever one does not yet exist, and you put a little flag in the final drawer to say "a complete code ends here." To check a code you follow the same letters; if any drawer is missing the code was never filed, and even if the path exists, it only counts as a full code if the end flag is set. To check a prefix you just confirm the letter path exists, flag or no flag.

**One line to remember:** Each edge is a character and each path is a prefix; a word-end flag distinguishes a full word from a mere prefix, and all operations are proportional to key length.

sections.s2_technical:
A trie node has two things: a way to reach child nodes by character and a boolean `isWord` that marks the end of a stored word. For lowercase letters you can use a fixed array of twenty-six child slots for speed, or a `HashMap<Character, TrieNode>` for flexibility with arbitrary characters. The map version is more general, so for banking reference codes with mixed characters I use `Map<Character, TrieNode> children`.

Insert walks the word character by character from the root. For each character you descend into the matching child, creating it if absent, for example `node = node.children.computeIfAbsent(c, x -> new TrieNode());`. After consuming the whole word you set `node.isWord = true` on the final node, which records that a complete word ends there. This is why two words sharing a prefix share nodes up to the point they diverge, which is where the space saving comes from.

Search also walks character by character, but if any character has no child you return false immediately, because the word is not present. If you consume the whole word, you return `node.isWord`, which is the crucial distinction: the path existing is not enough, the end flag must be set, otherwise you only stored a longer word that passes through here. The `startsWith` operation is the same walk but returns true as long as the path exists, ignoring the flag, because a prefix does not need a word to end exactly there.

A senior-level nuance is where tries beat hash sets. A hash set answers "is this exact word present" in constant time but cannot answer "does any word start with this prefix" without scanning everything. The trie answers prefix queries in key-length time, which is why it powers autocomplete, typeahead search, IP routing tables, and dictionary lookups. The cost is memory, since each node carries child pointers, and that is why compressed variants like radix trees collapse single-child chains to save space in production.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India has an internal console where staff type account reference codes, and the console must offer prefix-based autocomplete so a teller typing the first few characters sees whether any codes match. A hash set cannot answer prefix queries, but a trie can in time proportional to the prefix length. This is exactly what a prefix tree is for.

Problem 2 — The console must distinguish a complete valid code from a mere prefix of some longer code, so entering a prefix that is not itself a registered code must not be treated as a match. The word-end flag on each node makes that distinction exact.

In our mini-project we build a `ReferenceCodeTrie` with insert, search, and startsWith. The demo inserts a few reference codes, searches for a full code and a prefix-only string, and checks a prefix, logging each result.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: insert the codes "SAV", "SAV2001", and "CUR3001", then four queries.

Step 1: Insert "SAV". From the root we descend S, creating it, then A, then V. We set the end flag on the V node. The trie now has a path S-A-V with a word-end at V.

Step 2: Insert "SAV2001". We descend S, A, V, which already exist and are reused, then create 2, 0, 0, 1, and set the end flag on the final 1. The shared prefix "SAV" cost no new nodes.

Step 3: Insert "CUR3001". This shares nothing with the existing codes, so it creates a fresh path C-U-R-3-0-0-1 with the end flag on the last node.

Step 4: Search "SAV2001". We walk S, A, V, 2, 0, 0, 1, every child exists, and the final node has the end flag set, so we return true.

Step 5: Search "SAV2". We walk S, A, V, 2, every child exists, but the node at 2 does not have the end flag, because no code ends exactly at "SAV2"; it is only a prefix of "SAV2001", so we return false.

Step 6: startsWith "SAV" walks S, A, V, the path exists, so we return true regardless of the flag. startsWith "LOAN" fails at the very first character because the root has no L child, so we return false. All four operations touched only as many nodes as the query length.

```
[2026-10-26 23:28:01] INFO    search 'SAV2001' = true
[2026-10-26 23:28:01] INFO    search 'SAV2' = false
[2026-10-26 23:28:01] INFO    startsWith 'SAV' = true
[2026-10-26 23:28:01] INFO    startsWith 'LOAN' = false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```

  root
   ├─S─A─V*            (* = isWord)
   │     └─2─0─0─1*
   └─C─U─R─3─0─0─1*

  search  SAV2001 → path, end flag → true
  search  SAV2    → path, end flag → false
  starts  SAV     → path → true
  starts  LOAN    → no 'L' child → false
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Trie (Prefix Tree) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Tree of character edges; word-end flag per node             │
  │  Shared prefixes reuse nodes (structural sharing)            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: TrieNode stores structure; Trie exposes operations        │
  │  O: swap Map children for int[26] array without API change    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           ReferenceCodeTrie           │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  - root: TrieNode                     │
  │  + insert(word): void                 │  O(L)
  │  + search(word): boolean              │  O(L), path + flag
  │  + startsWith(prefix): boolean        │  O(L), path only
  │  - walk(s): TrieNode                  │  shared traversal
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘
                  │ composed of
                  ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │          TrieNode         │
  │  children: Map<Char,Node> │
  │  isWord: boolean          │
  └───────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Node role ─────────────────────────────

  [intermediate node] isWord=false (prefix only)
  [terminal node]     isWord=true  (complete word ends)

  ── Call Chain (search) ───────────────────────────────────

  1. search(word) → walk(word)
  2.   descend child per char; null → return false
  3. return node != null && node.isWord
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree in which each edge represents a single character and each path from the root spells a prefix, so words that share a leading prefix share the same initial path through the tree. Every node holds links to its children and a boolean that marks whether a complete word ends at that node. The beauty is that insert, search, and prefix checks all run in time proportional to the length of the key, completely independent of how many words are stored.

Insert walks the word character by character, descending into the matching child and creating it when it does not exist, and at the end sets the word-end flag on the final node. Search does the same walk but returns false the moment a character has no child, and if it consumes the whole word it returns the word-end flag, because the path existing is not enough; the flag must be set, otherwise I only stored a longer word that happens to pass through. The startsWith check is the identical walk but returns true as long as the path exists, ignoring the flag, because a prefix does not need a word to end exactly there.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used a trie to power prefix autocomplete for account reference codes in an internal staff console. A hash set could confirm an exact code instantly but could not answer "does any code start with these characters," whereas the trie answers that in time proportional to the prefix length. The word-end flag was essential so that typing a prefix that is not itself a registered code was not wrongly treated as a match.

The senior-level point I make is that the trie's strength is prefix queries, which is why it underpins autocomplete, typeahead search, IP routing tables, and dictionary lookups, all places where a hash set falls short. The trade-off is memory, because every node carries child pointers, so in production I would consider a compressed variant like a radix tree that collapses single-child chains, or a fixed array of children when the alphabet is small and fixed, to reduce the per-node overhead.
